title: After the Victory
subtitle: The Humaneness of Prisoners, the Ransom of Literacy, and the Shock in Makkah
summary: The dignified burial of the fallen, the Prophet addressing the fallen chieftains in the well of Badr, unprecedented humane treatment of seventy prisoners of war, the consultation on ransom, teaching literacy to Madinan children as a path to freedom, and the grief and vows of revenge in Makkah.

sections.text: When the dust settled over the valley of Badr, the full magnitude of the transformation became evident. Fourteen Muslim martyrs—six from the Muhajirun and eight from the Ansar—were lovingly laid to rest in honored graves on the battlefield. The bodies of the slain Makkan aristocracy, including Abu Jahl, Utbah, and Umayyah, were interred in an old, dry well (Qalib) to prevent desecration and disease.

Before the army departed on the third day, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ stood at the edge of the well and called the fallen persecutors by name: 'O Utbah ibn Rabi'ah! O Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah! O Umayyah ibn Khalaf! O Abu Jahl ibn Hisham! Have you found what your Lord promised you to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised me to be true.' When Umar ibn al-Khattab asked in wonder: 'O Messenger of God, do you speak to lifeless bodies?' the Prophet replied: 'By He in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, you do not hear what I say any better than they do, but they are incapable of replying.'
The quiet desert reaches where ethical standards of warfare were first established.

The Muslims marched back to Madinah escorting seventy prisoners of war, representing the elite of Makkah. In ancient warfare, captives were routinely tortured, mutilated, or sold into brutal slavery. The Prophet, however, issued an unambiguous command to his companions: 'I enjoin you to treat the prisoners with kindness' (Istawsu bi al-asara khayra).

The companions implemented this command with astonishing devotion. Abu Aziz ibn Umayr, brother of Mus'ab, later recounted: 'I was among the captives of Badr. Whenever the Muslims sat down to eat morning or evening meals, they would give me the bread while they ate only dates, out of obedience to the Messenger of God's injunction! Whenever a piece of bread fell into the hand of one of them, he would immediately hand it to me.'
Consultation on Ransom and the Price of Literacy

Upon reaching Madinah, the Prophet held a council of consultation regarding the fate of the seventy captives. Umar ibn al-Khattab advocated stern justice, arguing that these were the unrepentant leaders of tyranny who had tortured and exiled the believers, proposing that their own kin execute them. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, conversely, advocated mercy and reconciliation, saying: 'O Messenger of God, they are our cousins, kinsmen, and clan. I suggest that you accept ransom from them, which will strengthen us financially and perhaps God will guide them to Islam.'

The Prophet favored Abu Bakr's compassionate view, establishing ransoms between one thousand and four thousand dirhams according to each captive's wealth. For those who were destitute yet literate, the Prophet established a revolutionary condition: each literate prisoner could earn his complete freedom by teaching ten children of Madinah to read and write. Among the Ansari youths educated through this brilliant initiative was Zayd ibn Thabit, who would later become the principal scribe of the Quran.
The courtyards of learning in Madinah where literacy and knowledge were fostered.

The return to Madinah was accompanied by both jubilation and bittersweet grief. Zayd ibn Harithah and Abdullah ibn Rawahah had galloped ahead on the Prophet's camels to announce the victory. Yet as the army entered the oasis, they learned that the Prophet's beloved daughter Ruqayyah had passed away from severe illness while her husband Uthman ibn Affan nursed her, having remained behind under prophetic instruction.

In Makkah, news of the catastrophe struck like an earthquake. The sole survivor of the vanguard, Al-Haysuman ibn Iyas, rode into the city in shock. When the chiefs asked for news, he stammered: 'By God, we met them and it was as though we offered our shoulders to them to slaughter us as they pleased! Utbah is slain, Shaybah is slain, Abu Jahl is slain!'

Makkah plunged into paralyzed disbelief. Abu Sufyan, who now assumed sole leadership of Quraysh, strictly forbade all public wailing or lamentation, so that the Muslims would not rejoice at their sorrow. He swore a solemn vow never to apply perfume or approach his wives until he launched an expedition of vengeance. The victory of Badr had redefined Arabia: the myth of Quraysh's invincibility was shattered, and the seeds of the next monumental clash were sown.
